newsitem.title: USA: Families on edge as they wait for McVeigh verdict.
newsitem.headline: Families on edge as they wait for McVeigh verdict.

text.p: The rapid end to testimony in the Timothy McVeigh trial has surprised and delighted Oklahoma's bomb survivors but their nerves were on edge Thursday as they waited for the jury's verdict.

While prosecution attorneys made their closing arguments in a Denver courtroom on Thursday morning, officials said more than 180 survivors and relatives of those killed in the bombing gathered to watch the proceedings on a special telecast in Oklahoma City.
It was the highest attendance so far at the closed circuit link-up of the two-month trial taking place 600 miles away.
Others went about their daily routines, changed radically by the bombing two years ago, but stayed close to a radio or a television set so as not to miss the verdict when it comes in.

"It's up to the jury now. I'm getting excited about it, and nervous," said Patti Hall, 60, whose legs were crushed and lungs punctured when a truck bomb blew apart the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.

Virtually everyone in this city believes McVeigh is guilty of carrying out the attack, the worst ever on U.S. soil, and the surprise decision by his legal team to wrap up the defence case after just 3-1/2 days was interpreted here as demonstrating this was an open-and-shut case.
"I really expected more than that from Stephen Jones (the lead defence attorney)," Hall said. "If McVeigh wasn't guilty, he'd sure be fighting more to stay free."

Deb Ferrell, who lost her cousin and close friend Susan Ferrell in the bombing, has watched more than half the trial on the closed circuit feed being shown inside a Federal Aviation Administration auditorium on the outskirts of Oklahoma City.
Impressed by the prosecution's case, Ferrell knows exactly what she wants to hear from the jury.
"We want McVeigh found guilty. We feel he's the one, but you just never know what they will decide," she said.

Relatives of those killed would be appalled by an acquittal but Ferrell said the possibility "is in the back of all our minds" and that the nerves were getting to her. "I am in low- grade knots right now."
Oklahoma County District Attorney Robert Macy said he would respond to any acquittal by immediately requesting that McVeigh be kept in custody to face state murder charges here.

"We would go ahead and file a detainer on him and also file our charges against him," Macy said on Thursday. The charges at the trial in Denver refer only to the deaths of eight federal workers, but Macy has pledged to prosecute McVeigh for all 168 deaths if the federal case fails.
Maureen Bloomer, whose father, Olen, was killed in the bombing, said she believed the federal jury would convict McVeigh but might shy away from handing down a death penalty.

"I have this fear that Stephen Jones did a good enough job that he put a little doubt in their minds ... and they won't be able to give the death penalty," she told The Daily Oklahoman. "It'll be life in prison or something like that instead of taking him off the planet."

Ferrell said the prosecution's star witness, Michael Fortier, an old army buddy of McVeigh who testified that his friend told him he planned to bomb the federal building, was "pretty scummy" but that she believed he was telling the truth despite Jones' repeated attacks on his character and testimony.
"There is no reason to believe he was lying on the stand because his testimony, what he was talking about, fits well," she said.
The McVeigh trial began with jury selection just under two months ago and has raced along much faster than expected.

Angered by last year's decision to move the trial to Denver, survivors and relatives of the dead complained that their rights were being trampled on and Congress responded by passing a law that, for the first time, allowed a closed circuit feed of a federal trial.
But, while there is space for 330 people inside the auditorium and more than 180 showed up on Thursday, attendance over the course of the trial has averaged fewer than 100.

Paul Heath, a blast survivor and a psychologist, said people had stayed away because they work or are busy rebuilding their lives, or because they were scared graphic testimony would bring back a flood of painful memories.
"They just don't want to retraumatize themselves," Heath said.
